need_heading: What people searching for an EIS specialist usually need
need_lead: Most enquiries come from people weighing up an EIS investment or a company hoping to raise under EIS, and they want someone who deals with it regularly.
needs: You're an investor considering an EIS share offer and want someone to check it meets the conditions before you commit.
You run a company hoping to raise money under EIS and need advice on whether your trade and structure qualify.
You've been offered EIS shares through a broker or platform and want independent tax advice on the risk-to-capital condition.
You need help understanding how the funding limits apply to your proposed raise or to your investment.
You want a local adviser you can sit down with, rather than dealing entirely by email with an unfamiliar firm.
context_heading: What to understand before you choose
context: "Tax adviser" isn't a protected title in the UK, so anyone can use it. The Chartered Institute of Taxation (CTA) and the Association of Taxation Technicians (ATT) are the main specialist bodies, and many accountants and solicitors also advise on tax. Members follow Professional Conduct in Relation to Taxation, a shared code covering honesty, confidentiality and dealing with HMRC.

Tax advisers who charge a fee must be supervised for anti-money-laundering purposes, and HMRC has been tightening standards for paid tax agents. It's reasonable to ask about qualifications, supervision and professional indemnity insurance before you go ahead. Because you searched for the "best", judge for yourself: ask how often they handle EIS work, how they keep up with the risk-to-capital rules, and whether they've advised in your sector.

questions: How often do you advise on EIS, for companies and for investors?
Can you explain how the risk-to-capital condition applies to this particular opportunity?

Have you advised businesses in my sector before?
What qualifications and professional body memberships do you hold?
How do you charge for EIS advice, and what would you need from me to quote?

faqs.q: What does an EIS specialist actually check?
faqs.a: They look at the detailed conditions that apply to both the company and the investor, including the risk-to-capital rules and the funding limits. They can also flag where your own tax position interacts with the investment.

extra_heading: Making sense of "near me" when EIS advice is rarely local
extra: EIS work is niche, and the adviser who knows the risk-to-capital condition inside out may not be the one in your nearest town. "Near me" is a useful starting point, but it's worth asking whether the work can be done just as well remotely, with documents shared securely and meetings by phone or video. Many people find that a slightly longer journey, or no journey at all, opens up far more choice.

When you contact an adviser, ask directly how they handle the geographical side: do they meet in person, do they visit your business, or do they work entirely remotely? If you're a company raising money, you may also want to know whether they can attend meetings with your board or your investors, and whether that's included or charged separately. These practical details often matter more than a postcode.

Because you searched for the "best", remember that no directory or search engine can rank EIS specialists for your particular situation. The best adviser for you is the one who can explain the risk-to-capital rules in plain terms, has worked with companies or investors like you, and whose way of working suits you. Use the first conversation to test exactly that.

extra_faqs.q: Does my EIS adviser need to be local?
extra_faqs.a: Not necessarily. Much EIS advice can be handled remotely, and being open to advisers further afield may give you more choice. What matters is that you can communicate comfortably and that they understand your circumstances.

extra_faqs.q: How can I judge who is best for my EIS needs?
extra_faqs.a: Ask about their experience with EIS for companies and investors, how they keep up with the risk-to-capital condition, and whether they've advised in your sector. Also ask about qualifications, supervision for anti-money-laundering purposes, and professional indemnity insurance. Then decide which adviser gives you confidence.
